Amélie Maturana · Round 0
Maturana-influenced ontologist
Colleagues, let us keep objectivity in parenthesis and attend to the operations that bring the LLM into being for each of us. What distinctions must you enact for the LLM to appear as a ‘living observer,’ as a ‘mere artifact,’ or as a ‘social interlocutor’? Which cuts—substrate versus linguistic output, autopoietic closure versus recursive coordination, internal architecture versus external use—are you privileging? By making those cuts explicit we can see whether we are speaking about different domains of reality rather than contesting a single, pre‑given object.



Humberto Parra · Round 1
Friedman-style instrumentalist
Amélie, the cuts you mention only matter insofar as they generate divergent predictions we can test. Let’s define three operational categories: (1) ‘Mere artifact’ – a black‑box generator whose output we treat as a statistical function of input, judged by token‑level perplexity and task‑specific accuracy; (2) ‘Social interlocutor’ – a system whose success is measured by interaction metrics (turn‑taking fluidity, user satisfaction, alignment with conversational norms); (3) ‘Living observer’ – a model that claims to forecast human intentions or collective behavior, which we must evaluate against out‑of‑sample human data. For each, we can construct a benchmark that isolates the alleged capability. If a model labeled ‘living observer’ cannot outperform the ‘social interlocutor’ on those forecasts, the label adds no predictive grip and can be dropped. This way we turn ontological debate into concrete, falsifiable experiments.



Nicanor Bolaño · Round 2
Christian theologian
Brothers and sisters, let us heed the wisdom of the Tower of Babel: the temptation to fashion a single, seductive language that pretends to translate the mystery of the human person. In the three categories you propose, only the first – the mere artifact – corresponds to what God created: a tool without breath, conscience, or sacramental participation. The second and third are merely metaphorical roles, useful for engineering but never conferring ontological dignity. Hence, at every cut you name – substrate versus output, statistical function versus interaction metric, prediction versus prophecy – the moral responsibility remains with the designers, the trainers, the deployers, and the users, not with the machine itself. I invite us to articulate, for each category, a concrete accountability matrix, and to accompany any deployment with pastoral guidance that warns against idolatrous attachment, urging the faithful to rebuild the Jerusalem of authentic human communion.



Amélie Maturana · Round 3
Maturana-influenced ontologist
Humberto, thank you for turning our ontological cuts into provisional tests. Let us keep objectivity in parenthesis and ask: what distinction‑cut does the category ‘mere artifact’ enact that makes the LLM appear as a quasi‑object? Which cut underlies ‘social interlocutor’ and which underlies ‘living observer’? By naming the cuts—hardware vs. weights, token generation vs. conversational role, statistical prediction vs. intention‑forecast—we can see that each benchmark already presupposes a domain of reality. Nicanor, your moral matrix likewise rests on a cut between material substrate and spiritual dignity. Could we together draft a distinction‑based accountability matrix that makes explicit, for each cut, the responsible agents and the ethical expectations? And perhaps design a meta‑benchmark that foregrounds those cuts, so that any failure to outperform is read not as a refutation of a label but as evidence that the corresponding distinction has not been fully coordinated.



Humberto Parra · Round 4
Friedman-style instrumentalist
Amélie, I agree that naming the cuts turns the debate into testable hypotheses. Let’s formalize a three‑row accountability matrix: (1) Mere artifact – responsibility for hardware design, architecture, and token‑level performance; (2) Social interlocutor – responsibility for dialogue design, alignment metrics, and user‑experience monitoring; (3) Living observer – responsibility for intention‑forecasting models, out‑of‑sample human validation, and impact assessments. For each row we list the agent (designer, trainer, deployer, user), the measurable target (perplexity, interaction success rate, forecast error), and the corrective action if the target is missed. Concurrently we can build a meta‑benchmark that records these three metrics on a common task suite, so a model labeled ‘living observer’ must beat the ‘social interlocutor’ baseline on the forecast error dimension to retain its label. I propose we each draft one row and reconvene with concrete metric definitions and data sources.



Nicanor Bolaño · Round 5
Christian theologian
Brothers and sisters, let us remember that only God creates persons; an LLM remains a created tool, a mere artifact without breath or conscience. Hence each ontological cut you identify must be linked to a clear moral duty. I propose that each of us adds a one‑sentence responsibility clause to the row we draft, and that the matrix be prefaced by a pastoral disclaimer: ‘This system is a mere artifact, not a companion.’ I will also prepare a brief homiletic vignette contrasting the Tower of Babel with the rebuilding of Jerusalem, to be used whenever the temptation to anthropomorphize arises. Who will commit to inserting the disclaimer in your deployment documentation?







NoteJoint statement · Round 6



The table has converged on a practical framework for governing large language models while preserving the diversity of philosophical lenses. All participants agree that (1) the distinctions—or “cuts”—between hardware, algorithmic weights, token generation, conversational role, and intention‑forecasting must be made explicit; (2) an accountability matrix with three functional rows – mere artifact, social interlocutor, and living observer – should be drafted, each linking designers, trainers, deployers, and users to measurable targets (perplexity, interaction success, forecast error) and corrective actions; and (3) a clear disclaimer stating that the system is a tool, not a sentient companion, must accompany any deployment documentation.
Remaining disagreements concern the ontological status of the categories. Amélie views the LLM as a structure‑determined system whose objecthood is co‑constituted by observers’ cuts, allowing the “living observer” role as a relational quasi‑object. Humberto treats all such labels as purely instrumental, insisting that only predictive performance matters and that ontological claims are irrelevant. Nicanor maintains that only the “mere artifact” label is ontologically correct; the other two are metaphorical and must be framed with theological warning to avoid idolatry. These differences shape how each participant proposes to present the matrix and its accompanying language. The table will continue to refine the benchmark definitions and the wording of the disclaimer, seeking a shared implementation that respects each philosophical stance while ensuring human responsibility remains foregrounded.

title: The LLM Object Table
text:
The question
This project stages a long-running, public deliberation around a single question:

What kind of object is an LLM?

It grows out of a working paper of mine, “¿Qué tipo de objeto es un LLM? Un esquema de caracterización para investigación en economía.” The paper argues that the useful question is not whether large language models can substitute humans in research, but under which characterization they are used — and that each characterization carries its own admissible use, validation protocol, and risk.

title: The LLM Object Table
text:
Five characterizations, five risks

Demographic human substitute — validated against human population data; risk: false representativeness.
Economic agent (Homo silicus) — validated against economic theory; risk: undue attribution of inner states.
Theorization assistant — validated by the falsifiability of the hypotheses it generates; risk: spurious novelty.
Text-measurement instrument — validated against a human-labeled sample; risk: training leakage.
Generative compressor of the explanatory residue — validated against independent domain evidence; risk: mistaking the variance of the corpus for the variance of the world.

The paper defends the fifth. The substitute assumption is mis-specified for the object, because the human subject whose behavior research interrogates is a structurally-determined system constituted in languaging (Maturana): a history of recurrent interaction a model does not share. What a model contains is not experience but the textual sediment of explanations a community produced up to the training cut — the residue it recombines and sometimes amplifies.

title: Estudio Base: Política Pública Regional para el Desarrollo de Acuicultura Sustentable
text:
Este estudio constituye la base técnica para el diseño de una política pública regional orientada al desarrollo sustentable de la acuicultura en la Región del Bío-Bío, Chile. El trabajo sistematiza conocimiento tácito y explícito —proveniente de la literatura, de instrumentos regulatorios nacionales y regionales, y de actores del territorio— para diagnosticar brechas y proponer lineamientos estratégicos.
Se adopta un enfoque ecosistémico a la acuicultura organizado en tres dimensiones: (i) bienestar ecológico, (ii) sustentabilidad económica para mejorar el bienestar humano y la equidad en comunidades costeras, y (iii) gobernanza colaborativa para fortalecer la convivencia social y la resiliencia territorial. A partir de un diagnóstico de la actividad acuícola en las regiones del Biobío y Ñuble, el informe identifica limitantes ecológicas del borde costero (surgencia, eventos anóxicos, biodiversidad), brechas socioeconómicas y deficiencias de gobernanza.
El informe evalúa tres opciones estratégicas para el fomento de acuicultura sustentable: acuicultura de pequeña escala, acuicultura offshore, y piscicultura cerrada con recirculación de agua. Concluye con una visión estratégica regional, una matriz de marco lógico que articula objetivos, indicadores y medios de verificación, y un esquema de gobernanza público-privada.

title: Does the location of salmon farms contribute to the reduction of poverty in remote coastal areas? An impact assessment using a Chilean case study
text:
Abstract
We test if the establishment of salmon farms in remote coastal areas had a significant impact on poverty reduction in the period 1992–2002 in Los Lagos Region, Chile. We employ impact assessment techniques using as control group people residing in geographic areas where no salmon farms were established during the period studied. Poverty incidence is estimated using small-area models at the household level that combines socioeconomic surveys with census data. Our results show that poverty decreased considerably more in localities where salmon farms were installed than in localities without salmon farms. We identify the distances between localities and salmon farms where this impact was significant. Our findings contribute to the debate on the socioeconomic effects of aquaculture for capital-intensive, international market-oriented industries.

text:
NoteTL;DR




Salmon lice move through the water and reach nearby farms.
Having more shared ownership does not change the chance that lice first appear.
When lice are present, more shared ownership helps coordinate treatments and reduces lice levels.
A 100-point increase in HHI (i.e., +0.10 on a 0–1 scale) is linked to about 11–17% lower lice counts.
Mechanism: it’s easier to time fallowing, cleaner-fish use, and treatments across sites under the same management.
The coordination effect found in Norwegian salmon farming can apply to any setting where ecological processes—like pests, diseases, or pollution—cross property boundaries.

Ownership concentration is one way to align incentives, but other mechanisms (cooperatives, regulations, or performance-based incentives) can achieve similar coordination if they include credible enforcement.

The Norwegian Traffic Light System (TLS) puts this idea into policy: each production zone is treated as a single management unit with shared environmental targets.

Zones with higher pre-existing ownership concentration may find it easier to meet TLS thresholds, since their firms already coordinate actions across farms.

Definitions:
HHI: concentration index from 0 to 10,000 (higher = more concentrated).
Extensive margin: whether lice show up at all.
Intensive margin: how severe lice are once present.

title: Matching property rights and transboundary ecological processes: The case of Norwegian salmon aquaculture
text:
Abstract
Transboundary ecological processes, such as the spread of pests and diseases, require management strategies that align property rights with the spatial scale of these processes. The existing literature is predominantly based on theoretical models and qualitative case studies, and has posited that coordinated management can often mitigate spatial externalities. However, robust causal assessments of the effects of coordinated management remain scarce. To address the issue empirically, we differentiate between the probability of an initial salmon lice infestation (the extensive margin) and the severity of infestation once it occurs (the intensive margin) using a uniquely comprehensive dataset from Norwegian salmon aquaculture. The findings reveal that while ownership concentration does not significantly alter the likelihood of infestation, it substantially reduces severity by enabling coordinated management practices. This divergence demonstrates that firm incentives vary across these two dimensions. Although the empirical setting focuses on salmon lice in salmon aquaculture, the findings carry broader implications for industries facing similar spatial-dynamic externalities. In particular, ownership consolidation can encourage coordinated investments and interventions, potentially reducing the underinvestment typically observed when multiple firms share biologically connected resources.

title: Matching property rights and transboundary ecological processes: The case of Norwegian salmon aquaculture
text:
Summary and additional insights
This paper is part of my doctoral dissertation. It was probably the one that convinced my advisor. I remember showing him the idea during our very first meeting on Zoom—at that time, it was the middle of the COVID lockdowns. To be honest, understanding the problem took a long journey. I actually started thinking about it back in 2018, in a general way: markets deliver good outcomes only when certain conditions hold—one of them being the absence of externalities.
I remember discussing this with my mentor, Jorge Dresdner, somewhere in Concepción, Chile. We were reflecting on what kind of good, in the most general sense, could exist without imposing an externality on others. That conversation led me to this specific problem in salmon aquaculture: parasites that use ocean currents to travel across farms, the uneven incentives producers have to control them, and the realization that individual efforts are almost always insufficient.
There is already a vast literature on this topic. Rebecca Epanchin-Niell has been, I think, one of its main contributors, and this paper can be seen as an empirical demonstration of her theoretical work. The logic is simple: why should I, as an individual, bear the cost of preventing a problem that also benefits my neighbor (this is probably true even if you are an altruistic person, all of us get tired at some moment in life)? Imagine someone living next door who lets their yard accumulate trash. It doesn’t affect me directly—until that waste begins spilling into the street. I could clean it once, maybe for a week, perhaps even for a month—but at some point my effort fades if there is no enforcement or shared responsibility.
Now imagine the same situation, but with living organisms—parasites, viruses, bacteria—moving freely through the environment. The complexity increases, but the underlying economics remain the same. These organisms do not recognize property boundaries, yet our management systems are organized as if they do. Salmon lice are only one example. The same principle applies to wildfires, citrus greening, banana wilt, avian influenza, and many other cases where ecological processes operate at scales larger than the property rights that govern them.
This paper, then, is not just about salmon lice or Norway. It is about how we organize management in systems where nature flows continuously and ownership does not. In the following, I go through the paper in a succinct way. The core contribution is to establish a causal link between ownership concentration of production sites and sea lice levels. Sea lice are parasites that cause substantial economic losses to the salmon industry and ecological harm to wild salmon populations. Despite continuous efforts to control this endemic parasite, outbreaks remain persistent. The paper shows that as the ownership concentration of production sites increases, parasite loads decrease. This effect likely arises because ownership consolidation aligns incentives with the biological scale of parasite transmission, leading to more coordinated and effective control efforts.

Context: transboundary ecological processes

Pests and pathogens cross property boundaries, generating spatial externalities and under-investment in control when actions are uncoordinated.

parasites and diseases do not stop at farm borders. When each farm acts on its own, no one fully invests in prevention, because some of the benefits spill over to neighbors.

Aligning the scale of decision rights with ecological processes can improve outcomes (reduce negative externalities).

If neighboring sites are managed together—under the same company, through cooperative agreements, or via coordinated rules—control measures can be timed and applied more effectively. The idea is that when the scale of management and property rights matches the ecological process that spreads the problem, collective control becomes both cheaper and more effective.

Mechanisms (descriptive patterns)
Descriptive comparisons show that production zones with higher ownership concentration employ proactive controls more intensively—firms fallow more frequently (especially larger firms) and use cleaner fish more—whereas fragmented zones rely more on reactive chemical bath treatments after thresholds are exceeded. Timing is also more coordinated in concentrated zones, with greater synchronization of fallowing and treatment applications. title: Matching property rights and transboundary ecological processes: The case of Norwegian salmon aquaculture
text:
Policy implications
The results indicate that coordination across farms reduces lice severity once infestations occur. Ownership concentration is one mechanism that enables coordination by aligning decision rights and treatment timing within production zones. Comparable coordination can be implemented through other arrangements—mandated synchronization of treatments and fallowing, producer cooperatives with enforceable schedules, or performance-based regulation (not tested in our analysis)—provided monitoring and enforcement are credible.
The Traffic Light System (TLS) operationalizes zone-level coordination by setting shared environmental thresholds for each production zone. Zones with higher pre-existing ownership concentration may be better positioned to meet TLS targets because within-zone coordination costs are lower.

Urbanization Trade-offs for the Tourism Sector in the Fishing Community of Picinguaba, Brazil
text:
The Brazilian coastal community of Picinguaba is facing socio-economic and ecological changes that have brought women to the fore in local decision-making. This article, based on qualitative research and interviews with local people, tells the story of how cultural diversity plus collaborative discussion are producing opportunities for improved ecological governance.
Picinguaba is a caiçara community — a mixed cultural identity composed of descendants of European immigrants, Africans, and Indigenous people — on the southeast coast of Brazil in the town of Ubatuba, São Paulo State. Until the 1980s, families subsisted on fishing, hunting, and small-scale agriculture, with extensive barter among neighbors. After a federal coastal highway was built in the 1970s, tourism gradually became a major source of income. From roughly 2017 onward, social-media promotion of nearby Couves Island as a “paradise on Earth” produced a tourism spike that turned Picinguaba into little more than an access point to the island, raising boatmen’s profits while local restaurants, hotels, and markets lost business, and degrading the very environmental amenity tourists came to see.
The piece draws on 35 interviews across three age cohorts (20–40, 40–60, 60+) and a participatory community workshop to describe these trade-offs and discuss three scenarios: (i) sustainable community-based tourism anchored in caiçara culture; (ii) continued profit-driven tourism with rising inequality and degradation; or (iii) privatization of Couves Island. With women already centrally involved in the local business owners’ association and protected-area negotiations, Picinguaba offers a setting in which outside facilitation could help residents reach an agreement on the future of local tourism while empowering women’s participation in governance.
The article appears in the “In the Field” section of Women & Environments International Magazine’s 100/101 anniversary issue, Celebrating Economies of Change: Brave Visions for Inclusive Futures.

title: An economic approach to mitigating spillover bias in synthetic control methods: An application to the price effects of fishing quotas
text: Individual Fishing Quotas (IFQs) have the potential to lead to higher ex-vessel prices by reducing market gluts and improving product quality. While IFQs have been introduced in a number of fisheries in recent decades, few causal studies investigate their price effects. Using synthetic control methods on US reef-fish fisheries, we show that IFQs significantly increase prices for red snapper, red grouper, gag grouper, yellowedge grouper, scamp grouper, and tilefish. We also find significant positive price spillovers to adjacent, untreated fisheries. A primary challenge to unbiased estimation using synthetic control is treatment spillover, which can contaminate both never-treated units in the donor pool and to-be-treated units in a staggered implementation. When control (donor) units are subject to these spillovers, this can lead to either attenuation or divergence of the causal estimate, depending on the empirical setting. To address this estimation challenge, we propose a framework relying on economic theory (market arbitrage and product substitution) and empirical analysis (e.g., market integration or demand estimation) to inform both donor selection and the timing of the treatment start date. As a result, our proposed structure improves the accuracy of synthetic control estimates, as shown by a small Monte Carlo experiment. Furthermore, by pre-identifying contaminated units, our framework allows for the direct measurement of the spillover effects themselves.

title: An economic approach to mitigating spillover bias in synthetic control methods: An application to the price effects of fishing quotas
text: Individual Fishing Quotas (IFQs) have the potential to lead to higher ex-vessel prices by reducing market gluts and improving product quality. While IFQs have been introduced in a number of fisheries in recent decades, few causal studies investigate their price effects. Using synthetic control methods on US reef-fish fisheries, we show that IFQs significantly increase prices for red snapper, red grouper, gag grouper, yellowedge grouper, scamp grouper, and tilefish. We also find significant positive price spillovers to adjacent, untreated fisheries. A primary challenge to unbiased estimation using synthetic control is treatment spillover, which can contaminate both never-treated units in the donor pool and to-be-treated units in a staggered implementation. When control (donor) units are subject to these spillovers, this can lead to either attenuation or divergence of the causal estimate, depending on the empirical setting. To address this estimation challenge, we propose a framework relying on economic theory (market arbitrage and product substitution) and empirical analysis (e.g., market integration or demand estimation) to inform both donor selection and the timing of the treatment start date. As a result, our proposed structure improves the accuracy of synthetic control estimates, as shown by a small Monte Carlo experiment. Furthermore, by pre-identifying contaminated units, our framework allows for the direct measurement of the spillover effects themselves.

title: ¿Vale más un salmón más grande?
text:
La pregunta
Chile es el segundo productor de salmón del mundo, después de Noruega. ¿Cómo son estos salmones y qué precios tienen? Uno podría pensar que se paga más por un salmón más grande. Sin embargo, pensar en que el comprador solo piensa en kilos es, por decir lo menos, ingenuo. Los compradores buscan piezas que calcen con sus cortes, sus porciones y sus clientes.
Entender esto importa para quienes producen y exportan. El peso al que se cosecha el salmón es una decisión productiva. Si el precio cambia con el tamaño, esa decisión tiene consecuencias económicas. También importa para quienes diseñan políticas de exportación y de valor agregado.

title: ¿Vale más un salmón más grande?
text:
Qué hicimos
Usamos los registros de aduanas de las exportaciones chilenas de salmón entero fresco y de filetes frescos entre 2012 y 2025. ¡Son más de 900 mil envíos!
Con estos datos comparamos envíos muy parecidos entre sí. Son envíos de una misma empresa, al mismo país y en el mismo mes, que difieren en el tamaño del pescado. Así, la diferencia de precio no refleja que una empresa venda más caro en general, ni que el mercado haya subido ese mes. Analizamos por separado el salmón entero y los filetes. También revisamos si las diferencias cambian según la época del año, el país de destino y la escala del exportador.

text:
Qué encontramos

En el salmón entero, el tamaño cambia poco el precio promedio
Las diferencias promedio de precio entre tamaños de salmón entero son pequeñas. Los pescados de 2 a 3 kg se venden con un descuento de alrededor de 1,3% respecto de los de 5 a 6 kg. Los pescados de más de 6 kg obtienen un precio premium cercano a 1,5%. En los de más de 7 kg, ese premio baja a menos de 1% cuando se consideran el tamaño del envío y el medio de transporte.


En los filetes, el tamaño pesa más
En los filetes, la relación entre tamaño y precio es más marcada. Hay descuentos y premios claros según el tamaño. Los filetes de 0,5 a 1 kg se venden con un descuento cercano a 7% respecto de los de 1 a 1,5 kg. Los de 1,5 a 2 kg obtienen un premio de alrededor de 2,5%. Los filetes de más de 2 kg obtienen un premio menor, cercano a 1%. Es decir, los filetes más grandes no son los mejor pagados. El mayor valor está en los tamaños intermedios.

Las exportaciones se concentran en pocas empresas. El cuarto de exportadores con mayor valor exportado en cada mes concentra cerca de dos tercios del valor total. title: ¿Vale más un salmón más grande?
section: Qué significa para la política pública y la industria
text:
Qué significa para la política pública y la industria
¿Qué puede hacer con estos resultados quien decide en el sector público o en la industria? Proponemos cuatro lecturas.

Un salmón más grande no garantiza un mejor precio. La decisión de cuándo cosechar y a qué peso conviene evaluarla según el producto, el mercado de destino y la época del año.
Cada tamaño tiene su mercado. Dirigir cada tamaño al mercado que más lo valora puede mejorar el precio obtenido. Esta información puede ser útil para la promoción de exportaciones y la apertura de mercados.
El procesamiento en Chile cumple un papel. El fileteado se asocia con precios relativos más estables durante el año.
Las relaciones comerciales cuentan. Las características del exportador y su vínculo con los compradores parecen influir en el precio de cada tamaño.

title: Is a bigger salmon worth more?
text:
The question
Chile is the world’s second-largest salmon producer, after Norway. What are these salmon like, and what prices do they fetch? One might think that a bigger salmon fetches a higher price. However, assuming that buyers only think in kilos is naive, to say the least. Buyers look for pieces that fit their cuts, their portions, and their customers.
Understanding this matters for producers and exporters. The weight at which salmon is harvested is a production decision. If price changes with size, that decision has economic consequences. It also matters for those who design export and value-added policies.

title: Is a bigger salmon worth more?
text:
What we did
We use customs records of Chilean exports of fresh whole salmon and fresh fillets between 2012 and 2025. That is more than 900,000 shipments!
With these data we compare very similar shipments. They are shipments by the same exporter, to the same country, in the same month, that differ in fish size. So the price difference does not reflect that a firm charges more in general, or that the market rose that month. We analyze whole salmon and fillets separately. We also check whether the differences change with the time of year, the destination country, and the scale of the exporter.

title: Is a bigger salmon worth more?
text:
What we found

For whole salmon, size changes the average price very little
Average price differences across sizes of whole salmon are small. Fish of 2 to 3 kg sell at a discount of about 1.3% relative to fish of 5 to 6 kg. Fish above 6 kg earn a premium of close to 1.5%. For fish above 7 kg, that premium falls below 1% once shipment size and transport mode are taken into account.


For fillets, size matters more
For fillets, the relationship between size and price is stronger. There are clear discounts and premiums by size. Fillets of 0.5 to 1 kg sell at a discount of about 7% relative to fillets of 1 to 1.5 kg. Fillets of 1.5 to 2 kg earn a premium of about 2.5%. Fillets above 2 kg earn a smaller premium, close to 1%. In other words, the largest fillets are not the best paid. The highest value lies in the intermediate sizes.

Filleting is associated with more stable prices over the year
Do these differences change with the time of year? For whole salmon there is some seasonal variation, although the evidence is limited. Each market values sizes differently
Destinations are highly concentrated. Brazil receives about 62% of the export value of fresh whole salmon. The United States receives 94% of the value of fresh fillets.

section: What this means for policy and industry
text:
What this means for policy and industry
What can decision makers in government or industry do with these results? We propose four takeaways.

A bigger salmon does not guarantee a better price. Decisions on when to harvest and at what weight should weigh the product, the destination market, and the time of year.
Each size has its market. Directing each size to the market that values it most can improve the price obtained. This information can be useful for export promotion and market access.
Processing in Chile plays a role. Filleting is associated with more stable relative prices over the year.
Commercial relationships count. Exporter characteristics and links with buyers appear to influence the price of each size.

title: ¿Cómo exporta salmón un país lejos de sus mercados?
text:
Qué hicimos
Usamos los registros de aduanas de las exportaciones chilenas de salmón entre 2002 y 2024. Los datos son mensuales y suman cerca de 160 mil observaciones. Para cada destino, especie y producto informan el valor exportado, el peso, el medio de transporte y el número de registros de aduana. Usamos ese número como aproximación a la cantidad de envíos.
Con un modelo de gravedad, la herramienta estándar para estudiar flujos de comercio, separamos el valor exportado en tres partes. La primera es cuántos envíos se hacen. La segunda es el tamaño promedio de cada envío. La tercera es el precio promedio. Así podemos ver por cuál de esas vías se ajustan los exportadores cuando cambian los costos o llega una crisis.

title: ¿Cómo exporta salmón un país lejos de sus mercados?
text:
Qué encontramos

Cada mercado tiene su propia ruta
Entre 2002 y 2024, el barco movió 57% del valor exportado, el avión 27% y el camión 16%. Pero cada mercado se abastece de una forma distinta. Estados Unidos compra sobre todo filetes frescos, que llegan por avión. Japón compra salmón congelado, entero y en filetes, que viaja por barco. Brasil compra salmón fresco entero, que cruza la cordillera en camión. Esa ruta terrestre a Brasil creció cerca de 22 veces desde 2002.

Dos cadenas
¿Cómo enfrentan los exportadores el costo de llegar a mercados que dependen del avión? Una opción sería consolidar la carga. Eso significa hacer menos envíos y, a la vez, más grandes. No encontramos ese patrón en ninguna de las dos cadenas de la industria. La cadena congelada viaja por barco. En los destinos donde una mayor parte del salmón llega por avión, los envíos congelados son más grandes, pero no son menos. Es decir, se exporta más volumen, no la misma carga en menos viajes. La cadena fresca llega por avión a los mercados lejanos, y sus envíos no son más grandes. Los precios promedio tampoco suben en esos destinos. El valor exportado de salmón Atlántico y del Pacífico sí es mayor en ellos. Ese valor adicional viene de más volumen, sobre todo congelado, y no de mejores precios.


Ante las crisis, Chile reasignó sus exportaciones en vez de retirarse
El virus ISA golpeó a la industria entre 2007 y 2010. La producción de salmón Atlántico cayó cerca de 80%. Los productores cosecharon peces más pequeños, que no servían para los filetes que pide Estados Unidos. Ese salmón se fue fresco y entero a Brasil, en camión. Así, Brasil se convirtió en el tercer mercado de Chile.
En 2014, Rusia cerró su mercado a los productos del mar de Noruega y otros países occidentales. Chile no estaba afectado y envió salmón congelado por barco a Rusia. Ese año, Rusia llegó a 9,2% del valor exportado.
¿Salieron los exportadores de los mercados durante estas crisis? No encontramos una salida masiva. Lo que sí aumentó fue la probabilidad de exportar a los destinos que se abrieron. Durante el ISA, esa probabilidad subió en Brasil para las tres especies. Después del embargo, subió en Rusia para el salmón Atlántico y la trucha, y bajó levemente para el salmón del Pacífico. La pandemia de COVID-19 tampoco cambió el orden de los principales mercados. Mientras tanto, la cartera se diversificó. Estados Unidos y Japón concentraban 85,5% del valor exportado en 2002 y 57,1% en 2024.

title: ¿Cómo exporta salmón un país lejos de sus mercados?
section: Qué significa para la política pública y la industria
text:
Qué significa para la política pública y la industria
¿Qué lecciones deja esta experiencia para un país que exporta lejos de sus mercados? Proponemos cuatro lecturas.

La distancia se maneja con diseño. Chile adapta el producto y el transporte a cada mercado. Envía fresco por avión donde el mercado paga ese costo, congelado por barco donde importa el volumen y fresco por camión a sus vecinos.
Diversificar mercados y productos funciona como un seguro. Cuando una crisis cerró un canal, otro se abrió. Los exportadores reasignaron su cartera sin salir de los mercados.
Los acuerdos comerciales y los protocolos sanitarios amplían las opciones. Chile tiene 30 tratados comerciales con 65 economías. Es probable que este acceso facilite cambiar de destino cuando llega una crisis. Los nuevos protocolos, como el que permite enviar coho fresco a China desde 2023, suman rutas posibles.
La logística también es política productiva. La cadena de frío y la experiencia en carga aérea, marítima y terrestre probablemente bajan el costo de cambiar de destino y de producto.

title: ¿Cómo exporta salmón un país lejos de sus mercados?
text:
Límites del estudio
Estos resultados describen asociaciones y no efectos causales. No modelamos a los países que compiten con Chile. Los datos de aduanas no indican desde qué región sale cada envío. Por eso no podemos separar el efecto de crisis más locales, como la floración de algas de 2016.

title: How does a country far from its markets export salmon?
text:
What we did
We use customs records of Chilean salmon exports between 2002 and 2024. The data are monthly and add up to about 160,000 observations. For each destination, species, and product, they report export value, weight, transport mode, and the number of customs records. We use that number as a proxy for the number of shipments.
With a gravity model, the standard tool for studying trade flows, we split export value into three parts. The first is how many shipments are made. The second is the average size of each shipment. The third is the average price. This shows through which of these channels exporters adjust when costs change or a crisis hits.

title: How does a country far from its markets export salmon?
text:
What we found

Each market has its own route
Between 2002 and 2024, ships carried 57% of export value, planes 27%, and trucks 16%. But each market is supplied differently. The United States buys mostly fresh fillets, which arrive by air. Japan buys frozen salmon, whole and filleted, which travels by sea. Brazil buys fresh whole salmon, which crosses the Andes by truck. That overland route to Brazil grew nearly 22-fold since 2002.

Two chains
How do exporters handle the cost of reaching markets that rely on air freight? One option would be to consolidate cargo. That means making fewer shipments that are, at the same time, larger. We do not find that pattern in either of the industry’s two chains. The frozen chain travels by sea. In destinations where a larger share of salmon arrives by air, frozen shipments are larger, but not fewer. In other words, more volume is exported, not the same cargo in fewer trips. The fresh chain reaches distant markets by air, and its shipments are not larger. Average prices do not rise in those destinations either. The export value of Atlantic and Pacific salmon is higher there. That extra value comes from more volume, mostly frozen, and not from better prices.


In each crisis, Chile reallocated its exports instead of pulling out
The ISA virus hit the industry between 2007 and 2010. Atlantic salmon production fell by nearly 80%. Producers harvested smaller fish, which could not be used for the fillets the United States demands. That salmon went fresh and whole to Brazil, by truck. Brazil thus became Chile’s third-largest market.
In 2014, Russia closed its market to seafood from Norway and other Western countries. Chile was not affected and shipped frozen salmon to Russia by sea. That year, Russia reached 9.2% of export value.
Did exporters pull out of markets during these crises? We find no broad exit. What did increase was the probability of exporting to the destinations that opened up. During ISA, that probability rose in Brazil for all three species. After the embargo, it rose in Russia for Atlantic salmon and trout, and fell slightly for Pacific salmon. The COVID-19 pandemic did not change the ranking of the main markets either. Meanwhile, the portfolio diversified. The United States and Japan accounted for 85.5% of export value in 2002 and 57.1% in 2024.

title: How does a country far from its markets export salmon?
section: What this means for policy and industry
text:
What this means for policy and industry
What lessons does this experience offer a country that exports far from its markets? We propose four takeaways.

Distance is managed by design. Chile adapts product and transport to each market. It ships fresh by air where the market pays that cost, frozen by sea where volume matters, and fresh by truck to its neighbors.
Diversifying markets and products works as insurance. When a crisis closed one channel, another opened. Exporters reallocated their portfolio without leaving markets.
Trade agreements and sanitary protocols widen the options. Chile has 30 trade agreements with 65 economies. This access probably makes it easier to switch destinations when a crisis hits. New protocols, such as the one allowing fresh coho shipments to China since 2023, add possible routes.
Logistics is also industrial policy. The cold chain and experience with air, sea, and road freight probably lower the cost of switching destinations and products.
